newsitem.title: USA: Atlantis set for Thursday launch to Mir.
newsitem.headline: Atlantis set for Thursday launch to Mir.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis was set for a pre-dawn blastoff on Thursday after two minor technical problems were brushed aside, NASA officials said on Wednesday.
The shuttle was to soar aloft at 4:08 a.m. EDT (0808 GMT) to pick up U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger from Russia's Mir space station and drop off his replacement Mike Foale.
Launch pad workers at the shuttle's Florida launch site had overcome two minor technical glitches since the countdown began on Monday, shuttle test director Doug Lyons said.
Two electronic boxes that had shown strange readings during testing, but later appeared to be working properly, and some unexpected moisture in a rocket thruster had to be cleaned up.
The extra work slowed some launch pad work but was not expected to delay the liftoff.
"We are slightly behind, but during the course of the day we expect to make up that time and don't expect this to be an issue," he told a news conference on Wednesday.
Loading of the space shuttle's rust-coloured strap-on tank with super-chilled liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen rocket fuel was due to get underway at about 7 p.m. EDT (2300 GMT) Wednesday.
The shuttle's crew of seven, which includes a Russian woman and a French astronaut from the European Space Agency, were to start taking their seats aboard Atlantis at about 1 a.m. EDT (0500 GMT).

Forecasters were optimistic the weather would cooperate during the shuttle's short seven-minute launch window. "Conditions look good for getting off the ground tomorrow," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac said.
Atlantis was to dock with Mir on Friday night. Linenger, a 42-year-old U.S. Navy captain and medical doctor, has been working aboard the orbiting outpost since January.
His mission was marred by a brief but serious fire and a string of breakdowns in the station's life support systems.
Atlantis is carrying 4,000 lbs (1,814 kg) of supplies and equipment to Mir, including a new oxygen generator and repair gear to patch up a leak in the station's cooling system.
Foale, a British-born astrophysicist, will have a four-month tour of duty on Mir.
